papers.why: Read early and carefully: the nearest published work to the problem this list circles. papers.title: Inferring joint commitment from observed coordination
papers.citation_raw: Kuang, Brockbank, Bicchieri & Hawkins (2026). Inferring joint commitment from observed coordination. Proc. 48th CogSci.
papers.citation_html: Kuang, Brockbank, Bicchieri & Hawkins (2026). Inferring joint commitment from observed coordination. Proc. 48th CogSci.
papers.why: Hawkins again. Two experiments, N = 785, gridworld farm with an explicit stag hunt payoff structure (solo harvest of the center tree yields 1 berry, joint harvest 8). The model is Bayesian ToM over a latent commitment parameter θ ∈ [0,1] that interpolates between individual and collective expected utility — turning we-mode-vs-I-mode from a discrete model comparison into a fitted continuous dial. That single move is the most useful idea on this whole list.
flags: not dyadic — third-party observers rating pre-generated stimuli, N = 785 individuals
for commitment ratings the null model slightly beat the full model; only agreement ratings fit well (r = .90)

papers.authors_raw: Mon-Williams, Taylor-Davies, Mieczkowski, Vélez, Bramley, Wang, Griffiths & Lucas
papers.title: Partner modelling emerges in recurrent agents (but only when it matters)
papers.citation_raw: Mon-Williams, Taylor-Davies, Mieczkowski, Vélez, Bramley, Wang, Griffiths & Lucas (2025). Partner modelling emerges in recurrent agents (but only when it matters). NeurIPS 2025.

papers.why: Recurrent RL agents in Overcooked develop internal partner models — only when task structure makes partner-modeling instrumentally necessary. Read as an adversarial check on the obvious claims: an argument that human stag-hunt behavior requires recursive partner modeling has to clear what a non-recursive baseline already achieves. The null hypothesis, pre-built.

papers.authors_raw: Mieczkowski, Mon-Williams, Bramley, Lucas, Vélez & Griffiths
papers.title: Predicting multi-agent specialization via task parallelizability. arXiv:2503.15703

papers.citation_html: Mieczkowski, Mon-Williams, Bramley, Lucas, Vélez & Griffiths (2025). Predicting multi-agent specialization via task parallelizability. arXiv:2503.15703.
papers.why: An Amdahl's-Law account of when multi-agent systems should specialize vs. generalize, validated across SMAC, MPE and Overcooked. Note the boundary case: a stag hunt has parallelizability ≈ 0, since the whole point is that the stag requires simultaneous joint action. Useful as a theoretical foil rather than a direct tool — and it's a clean example of a simulation-experiment paper.

papers.title: The formation of social conventions in real-time environments
papers.citation_raw: Hawkins & Goldstone (2016). The formation of social conventions in real-time environments. PLOS ONE, 11(3), e0151670.
papers.citation_html: Hawkins & Goldstone (2016). The formation of social conventions in real-time environments. PLOS ONE, 11(3), e0151670.
papers.why: The one new item to read in Week 4 if nothing else. Real-time interaction produces more efficient and fairer conventions than simultaneous decisions, and high stakes amplify the effect. The methodological point is the one to steal: fine-grained movement trajectories reveal a continuous negotiation process that is completely invisible in discrete-choice data. An argument for continuous time as a measurement instrument, not a design flourish — and it's by a Ho co-author.

papers.title: The Stag Hunt and the Evolution of Social Structure
papers.citation_raw: Skyrms (2004). The Stag Hunt and the Evolution of Social Structure. Cambridge University Press.
papers.citation_html: Skyrms (2004). The Stag Hunt and the Evolution of Social Structure. Cambridge University Press.
papers.why: The modern theoretical treatment: risk-dominant (hare) vs. payoff-dominant (stag), and how network structure and signaling shift which one obtains. Where the paradigm is a stag hunt, this is the framing document. Chapters, not cover-to-cover.

papers.title: Coordination games in continuous time
papers.citation_raw: Zhao, S. (2020). Coordination games in continuous time. SSRN working paper.
papers.citation_html: Zhao, S. (2020). Coordination games in continuous time. SSRN working paper.
papers.why: The direct empirical case for continuous time: subjects coordinate significantly better, and reach the payoff-dominant equilibrium more often, than in discrete time — driven by faster within-round learning. Design evidence, to read before committing to a design.

papers.title: Linking compromise and responsibility attribution to risky decision-making in dyadic foraging
papers.citation_raw: Deng, … Garg & Mobbs (2026). Linking compromise and responsibility attribution to risky decision-making in dyadic foraging. PNAS. doi:10.1073/pnas.2602570123
papers.citation_html: Deng, … Garg & Mobbs (2026). Linking compromise and responsibility attribution to risky decision-making in dyadic foraging. PNAS. doi:10.1073/pnas.2602570123
papers.why: Arguably the closest paradigm match to a spatial stag hunt anywhere: 120 solo trials calibrating individual risk tolerance under predation, then 60 rounds of dyadic play where the avatar moves to the midpoint between both players' choices — a literal continuous compromise mechanism — plus post-hoc credit/blame attribution. Self-serving responsibility asymmetry predicts reduced willingness to compromise.
flags: partially verified — PNAS blocked direct fetch; confirm the full author list from the DOI before citing

papers.title: Herd those sheep: emergent multiagent coordination and behavioral-mode switching
papers.citation_raw: Nalepka, Kallen, Chemero, Saltzman & Richardson (2017). Herd those sheep: emergent multiagent coordination and behavioral-mode switching. Psychological Science, 28(5), 630–650.
papers.citation_html: Nalepka, Kallen, Chemero, Saltzman & Richardson (2017). Herd those sheep: emergent multiagent coordination and behavioral-mode switching. Psychological Science, 28(5), 630–650.
papers.why: Continuous spatial shepherding. All pairs start with divided-labor “search-and-recover”; a subset spontaneously discover a synchronized oscillatory mode. An entirely different theoretical vocabulary — dynamical systems, attractors, relative phase, HKB — describing the same phenomenon the Bayesian models describe. Read it precisely because it doesn't share their assumptions.

papers.citation_raw: Battalio, Samuelson & Van Huyck (2001). Optimization incentives and coordination failure in laboratory stag hunt games. Econometrica, 69(3), 749–764.
papers.citation_html: Battalio, Samuelson & Van Huyck (2001). Optimization incentives and coordination failure in laboratory stag hunt games. Econometrica, 69(3), 749–764.
papers.why: The “optimization premium” result: risk dominance alone doesn't predict behavior. Payoff details easily mistaken for arbitrary drive equilibrium selection — meaning the payoff matrix is a substantive theoretical commitment, not a parameter.

papers.title: Playing safe in coordination games: the roles of risk dominance, payoff dominance, and history of play
papers.citation_raw: Schmidt, Shupp, Walker & Ostrom (2003). Playing safe in coordination games: the roles of risk dominance, payoff dominance, and history of play. GEB, 42(2), 281–299.
papers.citation_html: Schmidt, Shupp, Walker & Ostrom (2003). Playing safe in coordination games: the roles of risk dominance, payoff dominance, and history of play. GEB, 42(2), 281–299.
papers.why: History of play strongly predicts future coordination, and fixed pairing beats random rematching. A direct design constraint: whether partners are stable across trials is a first-order manipulation, not a logistical detail.

papers.title: Strategic similarity and emergent conventions: evidence from similar stag hunt games
papers.citation_raw: Rankin, Van Huyck & Battalio (2000). Strategic similarity and emergent conventions: evidence from similar stag hunt games. GEB, 32(2), 315–337.
papers.citation_html: Rankin, Van Huyck & Battalio (2000). Strategic similarity and emergent conventions: evidence from similar stag hunt games. GEB, 32(2), 315–337.
papers.why: Conventions emerge in half of cohorts even with payoffs and labels scrambled every round — and when they do, they track efficiency rather than security or risk dominance. Evidence that people abstract strategic structure across surface variation, i.e. the “abstract goals” claim arriving from the economics side.

papers.authors_raw: Hallers-Haalboom, De Jaegher, Sterck, Brosnan & Vermande
papers.title: Communication increases cooperation among students in a coordination game
papers.citation_raw: Hallers-Haalboom, De Jaegher, Sterck, Brosnan & Vermande (2025). Communication increases cooperation among students in a coordination game. PNAS, 122(35), e2517669122.
papers.citation_html: Hallers-Haalboom, De Jaegher, Sterck, Brosnan & Vermande (2025). Communication increases cooperation among students in a coordination game. PNAS, 122(35), e2517669122.

papers.authors_raw: Möller, Unakafov, Fischer, Gail, Treue & Kagan

papers.citation_raw: Möller, Unakafov, Fischer, Gail, Treue & Kagan (2023). Human and macaque pairs employ different coordination strategies in a transparent decision game. eLife, 12, e80943.
papers.citation_html: Möller, Unakafov, Fischer, Gail, Treue & Kagan (2023). Human and macaque pairs employ different coordination strategies in a transparent decision game. eLife, 12, e80943.
papers.why: Transparency — mutual real-time observation of the partner's action — is what enables human coordination, and macaques largely don't exploit it. Directly relevant to any task that manipulates what partners see of each other, which most such tasks probably should.

papers.title: Joint control of visually guided actions involves concordant increases in behavioural and neural coupling
papers.citation_raw: Painter, Kim, Renton & Mattingley (2021). Joint control of visually guided actions involves concordant increases in behavioural and neural coupling. Communications Biology, 4(1), 816.

papers.why: Dual-EEG during joint cursor control, each partner controlling one dimension. The obvious bridge to the neuroscience side — this is what a neural measure of real-time coordination looks like.

papers.title: Collaborative hunting in artificial agents with deep reinforcement learning. eLife, 13, e85694
papers.citation_raw: Tsutsui, Shinya, Kudo, Müller & Lehmann (2024). Collaborative hunting in artificial agents with deep reinforcement learning. eLife, 13, e85694.
papers.citation_html: Tsutsui, Shinya, Kudo, Müller & Lehmann (2024). Collaborative hunting in artificial agents with deep reinforcement learning. eLife, 13, e85694.
papers.why: Role differentiation (chaser, blocker, ambusher) emerges from plain multi-agent deep RL with no theory-of-mind machinery. The deflationary alternative that has to be ruled out — cheap sophistication that looks like joint commitment.

papers.title: Gao, Newman & Scholl (2009) on the psychophysics of chasing · Keller, Novembre & Hove (2014) on rhythm in joint action · Konvalinka et al. (2010) on continuous mutual adaptation in joint tapping · Boesch & Boesch (1989) and Samuni et al. (2018) on chimpanzee cooperative hunting.
papers.citation_raw: Gao, Newman & Scholl (2009) on the psychophysics of chasing · Keller, Novembre & Hove (2014) on rhythm in joint action · Konvalinka et al. (2010) on continuous mutual adaptation in joint tapping · Boesch & Boesch (1989) and Samuni et al. (2018) on chimpanzee cooperative hunting.
papers.citation_html: Gao, Newman & Scholl (2009) on the psychophysics of chasing · Keller, Novembre & Hove (2014) on rhythm in joint action · Konvalinka et al. (2010) on continuous mutual adaptation in joint tapping · Boesch & Boesch (1989) and Samuni et al. (2018) on chimpanzee cooperative hunting.
papers.why: Background depth. The Gao one earns its place: people detect chasing rapidly and automatically from motion alone, so in a continuous spatial task partners are reading intentions off trajectories perceptually, below anything that would count as inference. Worth knowing before attributing all of it to a model.

papers.authors_raw: Deffner, Mezey, Kahl, Schakowski, Romanczuk, Wu & Kurvers
papers.title: Collective incentives reduce over-exploitation of social information in unconstrained human groups
papers.citation_raw: Deffner, Mezey, Kahl, Schakowski, Romanczuk, Wu & Kurvers (2024). Collective incentives reduce over-exploitation of social information in unconstrained human groups. Nature Communications, 15, 2683.
papers.citation_html: Deffner, Mezey, Kahl, Schakowski, Romanczuk, Wu & Kurvers (2024). Collective incentives reduce over-exploitation of social information in unconstrained human groups. Nature Communications, 15, 2683.
papers.why: The closest thing in either corpus to a payoff-structure manipulation in a real-time spatial task — the structural logic of a stag hunt (individual-safe vs. jointly-optimal) instantiated spatially and continuously. Individually-adaptive social information use turns out to be collectively harmful in concentrated environments; group-level incentives realign them. Also: 90m × 90m arena, restricted first-person FOV (108° × 76°), 25 Hz tracking of movement, proximity and visual attention. Copy that instrumentation spec.

thread.label: H · collective intelligence & social learning — Wu, Vélez

papers.title: Group coordination catalyzes individual and cultural intelligence
papers.citation_raw: Wu, Dale & Hawkins (2024). Group coordination catalyzes individual and cultural intelligence. Open Mind, 8, 1037–1057.
papers.citation_html: Wu, Dale & Hawkins (2024). Group coordination catalyzes individual and cultural intelligence. Open Mind, 8, 1037–1057.
papers.why: Wu's actual collective-intelligence position piece — and note the Hawkins co-authorship again. Argues the ad hoc interacting group is a distinct explanatory level between individual cognition and cumulative culture. This is the cleanest available statement of why dyad and small-group coordination is not just small-scale collective behavior, which is exactly the framing distinction this literature needs.

thread.label: H · collective intelligence & social learning — Wu, Vélez

papers.title: Humans flexibly integrate social information despite interindividual differences in reward
papers.citation_raw: Witt, Toyokawa, Lala, Gaissmaier & Wu (2024). Humans flexibly integrate social information despite interindividual differences in reward. PNAS, 121(39), e2404928121.
papers.citation_html: Witt, Toyokawa, Lala, Gaissmaier & Wu (2024). Humans flexibly integrate social information despite interindividual differences in reward. PNAS, 121(39), e2404928121.
papers.why: The formal-framework paper for the synthesis bullet. Four competing model families — asocial GP-UCB, Decision Biasing, Value Shaping, Social Generalization — arbitrated by exceedance probability. SG wins. The DB/VS/SG trichotomy maps directly onto the policy-level vs. value-level vs. belief-level places a partner can be inserted into a joint-planning model. A genuinely useful carve-up of the model space.

papers.title: Collaborative decision making is grounded in representations of other people's competence and effort
papers.citation_raw: Xiang, Vélez & Gershman (2023). Collaborative decision making is grounded in representations of other people's competence and effort. JEP: General, 152, 1565–1579.
papers.citation_html: Xiang, Vélez & Gershman (2023). Collaborative decision making is grounded in representations of other people's competence and effort. JEP: General, 152, 1565–1579.
papers.why: Vélez's most dyadic work, and the closest she gets to joint planning. In a stag hunt, “will my partner commit?” decomposes into exactly competence (can they?) and effort (will they bother?). The inference structure ports over. Caveat: turn-based offline-judgment tasks, not real-time — relevant model structure, irrelevant paradigm.

thread.label: H · collective intelligence & social learning — Wu, Vélez

papers.title: How do humans overcome individual computational limitations by working together? Cognitive Science, 47, e13232
papers.citation_raw: Vélez, Christian, Hardy, Thompson & Griffiths (2023). How do humans overcome individual computational limitations by working together? Cognitive Science, 47, e13232.
papers.citation_html: Vélez, Christian, Hardy, Thompson & Griffiths (2023). How do humans overcome individual computational limitations by working together? Cognitive Science, 47, e13232.
papers.why: Her best short piece for the synthesis bullet — reframes human cognition as a distributed computing system, with a particle-filtering model of populations approximating Bayesian inference via cultural accumulation. Read for framing, not for a fittable model: it's a population/multigenerational argument, not a dyadic one.

thread.label: H · collective intelligence & social learning — Wu, Vélez

papers.title: Learning from other minds: an optimistic critique of reinforcement learning models of social learning
papers.citation_raw: Vélez & Gweon (2021). Learning from other minds: an optimistic critique of reinforcement learning models of social learning. Current Opinion in Behavioral Sciences, 38, 110–115.
papers.citation_html: Vélez & Gweon (2021). Learning from other minds: an optimistic critique of reinforcement learning models of social learning. Current Opinion in Behavioral Sciences, 38, 110–115.
papers.why: Six pages, high value-per-minute. Argues RL models of social learning oversimplify by treating social information as a lean reward-predictive cue when humans instead infer latent goals, beliefs and strategies; advocates hybrid Bayesian-ToM + RL. That is the argumentative bridge between the economics/RL framing and the cogsci-ToM framing this list sets out to synthesize.
